# Installation

## Nightly builds

Every push to the `root` branch builds BlitzLLVM for Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (arm64) and publishes the result as the `nightly` release: https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/releases/tag/nightly

1. Download the zip for your platform (`blitzllvm-windows-x64.zip`, `blitzllvm-linux-x64.zip` or `blitzllvm-macos-arm64.zip`).
2. Extract it anywhere. The layout is:

   ```
   bin/blitzcc          the compiler (blitzcc.exe on Windows)
   bin/blitz-format     formats source code, see [[blitz-format]]
   bin/runtime/         the runtime library, keep it next to blitzcc
   userlibs/            user libraries
   ```

3. Optionally add the `bin` directory to your `PATH`.

Tagged releases are published at https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/releases with the same files, see [[Releasing]].

If you built it yourself, `cmake --install` produces the same layout, see [[Building]].

## Clang

BlitzLLVM writes LLVM IR and hands it to `clang`, which has to be installed and on your `PATH`. Use another one with `--cc <path>` or the `BLITZLLVM_CC` environment variable.

* Windows: install LLVM from https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/releases, or the "C++ Clang tools for Windows" component of Visual Studio.
* Debian and Ubuntu: `sudo apt-get install clang`
* macOS: `xcode-select --install`

## Graphics

Programs draw through Vulkan 1.3 into an SDL3 window, so a Vulkan 1.3 capable driver has to be installed. The Vulkan loader is loaded when the program starts, and the result is still a single executable. Set `BLITZ_HEADLESS=1` to run a program without a window or GPU.

## Your first program

Save this as `hello.bb`:

```
Print "Hello from BlitzLLVM"
```

and run it (blitzcc builds it in a temporary directory and runs it, like the original), or build an executable:

```sh
blitzcc hello.bb
blitzcc -o hello hello.bb
./hello          # hello.exe on Windows
```

Useful options:

```sh
blitzcc program.bb              # build and run right away (arguments for the program go after --args)
blitzcc -o program program.bb  # only build the executable
blitzcc -O2 -o program program.bb   # a lower optimization level (the default is -O3)
blitzcc --fast-math full -o program program.bb   # also assume that Float math never produces NaN or Infinity (see below)
blitzcc -S program.bb          # only write the LLVM IR (program.ll)
blitzcc --target <triple> program.bb   # cross-compile
blitzcc -q program.bb          # quiet: no version banner and no warnings
blitzcc -W4 -Werror program.bb   # more warnings (-W0 to -W4, -W2 is the default), and any warning is an error, see [[Warnings]]
blitzcc -Wno-implicit-lossy-real-to-int program.bb   # turn off one warning
blitzcc +q program.bb          # very quiet: no messages from the compiler at all, errors included (it still returns a non-zero exit code)
blitzcc -c program.bb          # compile only: check the program, don't create an executable (unless -o is given)
blitzcc -d program.bb          # debug: no optimization, with debug information (DWARF, or CodeView for Windows MSVC)
blitzcc -g -O2 program.bb      # debug information in an optimized build
blitzcc --console -o program program.bb   # Windows: a console program (by default programs have no console window, see [[Differences]])
blitzcc -k                     # list all keywords, runtime functions and userlib functions
blitzcc +k                     # same, with the syntax of the functions
blitzcc -v                     # print the version
```

`-v` prints the version; the verbose output of the commands that are run is `--verbose`. The userlibs for `-k` and `+k` are the `.decls` files in `userlibs` next to `bin` (or in `share/blitzllvm/userlibs`), or in the directory given with `--userlibs-dir`.

Userlibs work like they do in Blitz3D: a program that calls a function from a `.decls` file loads the library it names when it runs, with `LoadLibrary` (Windows) or `dlopen` (Linux, macOS), and looks the function up with `GetProcAddress` or `dlsym`. The library is loaded on the first call of one of its functions, so it does not have to exist when the program is built. It is looked for in the userlibs directory, next to the program, next to the source file, and then by the system, so `user32.dll` or `libm.so.6` work without being copied anywhere. The name in the `.lib` line is tried as written, and with the extension of the platform (`mylib.dll` finds `libmylib.so` or `libmylib.dylib`), so one `.decls` file works everywhere. If the library or the function can not be found, the program stops with a runtime error when the function is called. The directory is `--userlibs-dir`, then the environment variable `BLITZLLVM_USERLIBS`, then the one of the installation. Functions use the C calling convention; strings are C strings, banks and objects are passed as the address of their memory, and a decorated name (`_Name@8`) falls back to `Name` if the library does not export it as written. Static libraries (`.a`, `.lib`) can not be loaded this way.

`blitzcc --help` lists all of them.

### Optimization

Programs are built with `-O3` and loop unrolling by default; `-d` builds without optimization. Float math is compiled with the LLVM fast-math flags `reassoc nsz arcp contract afn` (`--fast-math safe`, the default), which allows reordering, fused multiply-add and reciprocal math. Results may differ from the original in the last digits. `--fast-math full` also assumes that NaN and Infinity never occur, which makes checks like `x <> x` (is this NaN?) always false, so it is opt-in. `--fast-math off` keeps exact IEEE behavior. The default targets a generic CPU of the architecture; add `--llvm-flag -march=native` for a program that only runs on the machine that built it.
